title: How to use waste canvas for cross-stitch
subtitle: Stitching a counted design onto a fabric without a woven grid
excerpt: Waste canvas is a coarsely-woven grid canvas that is basted onto plain fabric to provide a counted grid for cross-stitch on surfaces that have no natural grid of their own. Once the stitching is complete, the canvas threads are dampened and pulled out individually, leaving the design embedded in the base fabric.
sourceNotes: Waste canvas technique. Documented in major cross-stitch publisher guides. Standard practice for stitching onto cotton, linen, canvas, and denim that has no inherent grid.

glossaryTerms.definition: The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch.

content.text: Waste canvas lets you work a counted cross-stitch design onto any plain fabric that has no grid of its own: a cotton tote, a linen tea towel, a denim jacket, a pocket. The canvas provides the grid for counting while you stitch through it into the base fabric beneath. When the stitching is done, you wet the canvas and pull the threads out, leaving only the

Cut a piece of waste canvas at least 3 cm larger than the stitched design on each side. Position it on the base fabric where you want the design to sit and pin it in place. Check that the canvas grid is square to the fabric grain of the base cloth, not at a diagonal.
Baste the canvas to the base fabric around the edges with a simple running stitch in a contrasting thread. The basting keeps the canvas from shifting as you stitch through it.

Stitch the design using the canvas grid as the counting guide. Use a sharp needle rather than a tapestry needle, because you are piercing the base fabric. Push the needle through the canvas hole and into the base fabric, then back up through the adjacent canvas hole. Each stitch passes through both layers.
When the stitching is complete, dampen the waste canvas with clean water. The canvas has a sizing agent that dissolves when wet, making the canvas threads go soft and loose.

Remove the basting threads. Use tweezers or your fingernails to pull out the canvas threads one at a time, gripping each individual thread and sliding it out from under the stitches. Work slowly; hurrying tears the base fabric or catches the floss. The canvas threads should come free without resistance once the sizing is wet.

Check the design from the front when all canvas threads are removed. The stitches should lie smooth on the base fabric, the cross shape clear and even. If any stitches were pulled out of position, press gently from the back with a damp cloth and steam to set them.

items.symptom: Canvas threads won't pull out cleanly after dampening
items.cause: The canvas is not wet enough, or the sizing has not dissolved fully.
items.fix: Apply more water with a sponge and wait a minute for the sizing to soften. If the canvas is still stiff, soak a cloth in warm water and lay it over the area for 30 seconds before trying again.

items.symptom: Stitches distort when canvas threads are pulled out
items.cause: The canvas threads are being pulled at an angle and catching the floss.
items.fix: Always pull each canvas thread straight along its own axis, not sideways. Pull horizontals horizontally and verticals vertically. Use tweezers to grip each thread close to the fabric surface.

content.text: A tote bag or tea towel with a small cross-stitch design is a practical first waste-canvas project. The base fabric is washable and the waste canvas removal is straightforward. Avoid very open-weave fabrics for a first attempt; denim or a firm cotton gives the cleanest result.
